title: Abdominal pain and drowsiness on a second ED visit

source.citation: Singh M, Bloom J, Howland MA, Biary R, Su M. Delayed Diagnosis Salicylate Toxicity With Confirmed Cerebrospinal Fluid Salicylate Concentration: A Case Report of Altered Mental Status Without Neuroglycopenia and With Coagulopathy. Cureus. 2025;17(8):e89613.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Abdominal pain and altered mental state
presentation.hpi: Previously healthy. She was seen at another hospital the day before for the same symptoms, where blood tests were reportedly normal and a CT (body region unclear) was unremarkable; this history cannot be verified. The abdominal pain has worsened since. She does not mention having taken anything.
meds: No reported use of oral anticoagulants, vitamin K antagonists or heparin

exam: Later in the ED: new fever of 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) and worsening altered mental status

investigations.name: CSF (lumbar puncture at 4.5 h)
investigations.value: Clear; WBC 0/mm³, RBC 1/mm³, glucose 60 mg/dL, protein < 10 mg/dL

investigations.name: Salicylate (serum, first measured 25 h after arrival)

imaging.finding: Radio-opaque foreign bodies in the colon, consistent with pill fragments

diagnosis.primary: Salicylate poisoning (aspirin ingestion about 36 h before arrival), diagnosed late, with encephalopathy and coagulopathy
differentials: Toxic alcohol ingestion (methanol or ethylene glycol)

management: CT head, then lumbar puncture 4.5 h after arrival to exclude meningitis
Re-interviewed after CT showed pill fragments: she admitted taking an unknown number of aspirin tablets about 36 h before arrival
IV sodium bicarbonate on poison center advice, alkalinizing serum and urine (urine pH > 8)
Prothrombin complex concentrate 2,500 units before dialysis catheter placement, correcting the coagulopathy
Hemodialysis 37 h after arrival for suspected salicylate encephalopathy
outcome: Serum salicylate fell to below 1 mg/dL with bicarbonate and hemodialysis. Abdominal pain and encephalopathy resolved by hospital day 4; medically cleared with no deficits and transferred to inpatient psychiatry.
teachingPoints: Salicylate poisoning is easily missed when the history is withheld; unexplained high anion gap acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, altered mental status or fever should prompt a salicylate level.
Check the PaCO2 against Winter's formula (1.5 × HCO3⁻ + 8 ± 2): a PaCO2 well below the expected value means a concurrent primary respiratory alkalosis, the classic salicylate pattern.
Altered mental status in salicylate poisoning is an indication for hemodialysis regardless of the level (EXTRIP salicylate recommendations); bicarbonate alone is not enough.
Alkalinize with IV sodium bicarbonate to a urine pH of 7.5–8.0 while replacing potassium; avoid intubation if possible, and if it is unavoidable, keep minute ventilation high.
Salicylate can prolong the PT/INR by reducing vitamin K-dependent factors, on top of its antiplatelet effect; bezoars or pill fragments delay absorption, so repeat levels until they fall.

questions.q: Which test is most likely to explain this presentation?
questions.extra: Na⁺ 134, Cl⁻ 101, HCO3⁻ 14 mmol/L (anion gap 19), glucose 87 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, WBC 23 x10³/µL. ABG: pH 7.39, PaCO2 23.1 mm Hg, HCO3⁻ 17 mmol/L, base excess −10.9. CSF clear, 0 WBC. CT abdomen: radio-opaque fragments in the colon.
options: Serum osmolality for an osmolal gap
Repeat lumbar puncture with viral PCR
questions.explanation: For an HCO3⁻ of 17, Winter's formula predicts a PaCO2 of 31.5–35.5 mm Hg; 23 mm Hg means a primary respiratory alkalosis on top of a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, the classic salicylate pattern. With pill fragments on CT and unexplained encephalopathy, a salicylate level is the key test; toxic alcohols cause only compensatory hyperventilation. Here the level was first sent 25 h after arrival.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate management now?
questions.extra: Serum salicylate 48.8 mg/dL. She remains lethargic with altered mental status. Urine pH 5.5, K⁺ 3.9 mmol/L, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL.
options: Bicarbonate alone, as the level is below 100 mg/dL
IV sodium bicarbonate and emergency hemodialysis
Rapid sequence intubation to protect the airway
questions.explanation: Altered mental status is an indication for extracorporeal removal regardless of the concentration (EXTRIP salicylate recommendations), so she needs bicarbonate (urine pH 7.5–8.0, with potassium replacement) and hemodialysis. Intubation removes her protective hyperventilation and can cause abrupt deterioration; if unavoidable, hyperventilate and give bicarbonate. Charcoal alone is inadequate.

questions.q: Before dialysis catheter placement her clotting tests are abnormal. What is the most likely mechanism?
questions.extra: PT 63 s, INR 5.52, aPTT 40.2 s. AST 17 U/L, ALT 15 U/L, bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, platelets 371 x10³/µL. No anticoagulant use reported.
options: Salicylate-induced fall in vitamin K-dependent factors
Acute liver failure from occult paracetamol co-ingestion
Dilution of clotting factors by bicarbonate infusion
questions.explanation: Besides irreversibly inhibiting platelet cyclooxygenase, salicylate lowers vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX and X) in a warfarin-like way, prolonging the PT/INR more than the aPTT. Normal transaminases and bilirubin argue against liver failure, and a normal platelet count against DIC. Prothrombin complex concentrate corrected it before the catheter was placed.

evidence.quote: An 18-year-old healthy female patient presented to an emergency department (ED) with abdominal pain and an altered mental state
she was seen at a different hospital for the same symptoms one day prior with reportedly normal laboratory tests and an unremarkable CT imaging of an unspecified body part(s)
According to the patient's history (which could not be verified)
Her abdominal pain had worsened since her prior visit.
She did not initially report salicylate overdose.
despite normal hepatic function and lack of reported use of oral anticoagulants, vitamin K antagonists, or heparin

the patient underwent a transvaginal ultrasound two hours after ED presentation for abdominal pain that visualized a right ovarian cyst
She also had an unremarkable CT brain scan that was ordered due to altered mental status.
She underwent a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, which noted radio-opaque foreign bodies in the colon that were deemed to be consistent with "pill fragments"
On re-interview, the patient confirmed taking an unknown quantity of aspirin pills approximately 36 hours before arrival to the second hospital.
A serum salicylate concentration obtained at 25 hours after the second ED presentation resulted in a value of 48.8 mg/dL (therapeutic range: 15-30 mg/dL).
The regional poison center was consulted and recommended treatment with IV sodium bicarbonate, and the patient's urine and serum were adequately alkalinized (urine pH > 8).
Hemodialysis (HD) was also recommended due to a concern for salicylate-induced encephalopathy.
Hemodialysis (HD) was performed 37 hours after ED presentation due to the altered mental state.
Prothrombin time was 63 seconds (reference range: 11-13 seconds), international normalized ratio was 5.52 (reference range: 0.8-1.1), and activated partial thromboplastin time was 40.2 seconds
The patient was administered 2,500 units of prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) before catheter placement, which corrected the coagulopathy
The patient's serum salicylate concentration decreased with sodium bicarbonate infusion and HD
After the conclusion of this case, waste CSF from the patient's lumbar puncture from hospital day 1 was tested for salicylate concentration. The CSF salicylate concentration was 23 mg/dL
On hospital day 4, the patient's abdominal pain and encephalopathy resolved. She was medically cleared with no noted deficits and transferred to the inpatient psychiatry service.
